body.text: In short:
A new report has found the absence of a national definition for what constitutes an assistance dog is fuelling discrimination and undermining their legitimacy.
It also found fragmented provider and training standards are contributing to access refusals.
What's next?
Several solutions have been proposed to bolster community trust and educate the public.
Ollie Andrews's assistance dog Orla provides the army veteran with support and independence.
But she also makes him the target of "infuriating" discrimination in places like an outback cafe they tried to visit recently on a trip to South Australia.
"The owner basically said we weren't welcome to stay inside the cafe with her because he didn't want to set a precedent for all his customers that had farm dogs," Mr Andrews said.
"I showed him all the documentation that we have, an ID card that has my photo on there, her photo and South Australian legislation on the back of it, but he still wasn't having a bar of it."

Getting Orla legally recognised as an assistance animal was a rigorous process that included a medical assessment, getting her properly trained, and then accredited through Assistance Dogs International (ADI).

"She can sense if I'm getting nervous. She'll come up and she'll like nudge my thigh with her nose and make eye contact with me. That forces me to stop, slow down, think about what I have to do and she'll keep doing that … until I'm a bit calmer," Mr Andrews said.
Thousands of Australians use assistance dogs but there is widespread confusion about the critical role they play.

A new report, prepared by research firm Mandala for ADI, has found there is broad scepticism about the use of assistance dogs because there is no national definition of what they are and no requirement for formal accreditation.
"[The inconsistency] makes it harder for businesses to understand their legal obligations relating to assistance animals," the report said.
"It makes it harder to enforce these obligations to uphold the rights of handlers. And it makes it harder to build public trust in the assistance dog system."
While it is illegal to refuse service to someone with an assistance animal, such incidents are frequent, particularly during taxi and rideshare trips, air travel, and in hospitality venues.

Fifty-eight per cent of assistance dog handlers in Australia experienced an access refusal in the past year, according to the report, and almost 60 per cent said they considered avoiding public places altogether, compared with 40 per cent globally.
A patchwork of rules
Anyone can train an animal to be a companion, but the process of having it legally considered an assistance animal is different depending on where people live.
Some systems require medical checks for handlers, and while some bodies issue their registered animals with ID cards, others do not.

The federal Disability Discrimination Act contains three different definitions and state-based legislation also varies. Some states define assistance animals or dogs, while Tasmania only defines a guide dog.
States also apply different standards for providers, meaning an assistance dog accredited in one state may not be recognised in another.

The report found at least 1,000 dogs were placed with Australians with disability in 2025, but only about 25 per cent came from providers accredited by ADI or the International Guide Dog Federation, which ensures training reflects established global best practice.
The remaining 75 per cent, about three in four of all assistance dogs placed in 2025, were trained by other organisations "to varying and often unknown standards".
That did not mean those dogs were poorly trained, but it was difficult to immediately verify the level of training they had, the report said.
"A handler may have a dog that's had some training, but a venue owner or driver has no way of knowing that," Mandala partner Tom McMahon said.
Issue to persist without change, advocates say
Ashley De Silva, CEO of Guide Dogs New South Wales/ACT, said handlers should not have to "prove over and over again that [they] belong".
He said businesses often lost trust in the assistance animal system after experiences with one not "trained to the standard you would expect".
"That is a real concern because what happens for them is they start to doubt that the next time someone comes to their venue, they won't have similar issues," he said.
The report proposed five solutions to the issue, including creating a single national legal definition of assistance dogs and public education to ensure the wider community could recognise them.
"A cafe owner or an Uber driver shouldn't have to guess," ADI Oceania chair Damian Papps said.
"It's about giving certainty to people with disability and the businesses and transport operators that serve them."
Mr de Silva said assistance dog handlers would continue to be unfairly "tested at the door" until more standardisation occurred.
The full recommendations:
• one national legal definition of an assistance dog, aligned with international standards
• national standards for all assistance dogs, including animal welfare requirements
• national accreditation for trainers and a single national identity card for handlers
• a pathway for all trainers and providers to join an international accreditation framework
• public education, and a national process for resolving access complaints
